newsitem.title: USA: GM Canada strike to affect U.S. economy -- experts.
newsitem.headline: GM Canada strike to affect U.S. economy -- experts.

text.p: As if to illustrate the adage that what is good for General Motors is good for the country, economists said a Canadian autoworkers' strike against G.M. -- if it lasts -- could crimp U.S. economic growth in the fourth quarter.

A strike of any length will also tend to soften U.S. economic numbers, experts said, blurring the picture of the U.S. economy and possibly making it less likely that the Federal Reserve will alter interest rate policy this calendar year.

"It will be harder for the Fed to do anything because we will be less certain about what is going on in the economy,' said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "In that sense, it would lend support to policy makers arguing, 'Well, let's wait.'"

GM's 26,000 Canadian Auto Workers union members launched an escalating strike on Oct. 3 that shut all of GM's Canadian production on Oct. 9. On Tuesday, GM said the Canadian walkout had forced it to idle more than 10,000 of its workers in the United States and Mexico.
"So far, the effects of the Canadian strike on the U.S. economy have been small," Feinman added. "But if the strike were to last a few more weeks, the effects would multiply."
Feinman said since GM output comprises about 1.0 percent of U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP), big changes in the automaker's production levels are significant.
"In the economic numbers, you're talking about changes (in output), so if 1.0 percent of your economy disappears, your growth rate is going to look pretty sick," Feinman said.
The first data to reflect the impact of the Canadian walkout will be auto assembly rates, noted Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A.

But how much of a production drop that will be is not entirely clear because the auto industry, itself, had already scheduled lower production in the fourth quarter as they prepared for a strike, Bhagavatula said.

"In July and August, the automakers overproduced relative to the sales pace for those two months," he said. "The idea was to fill up dealer lots before going into negotiations with the UAW (United Auto Workers)."
Since few of the U.S. layoffs had taken place before the latest data were collected on new unemployment claims, the laid-off autoworkers should not show up in the jobless claims data due on Thursday.
But that picture could soon change.
"Starting next week you could start to see it in the new jobless claims figures," said Feinman.

The GM layoffs are unlikely to affect the October employment report that the government will release on Friday, Nov. 1, because the reference week for the payroll data ended on Saturday, Oct. 12, economists said.

"In theory, you're in a pocket," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "You're past the survey week for October payroll data and if the strike were settled in a week or two, you'd have a strong likelihood that laid-off workers would return to the payrolls by early November and you'd have no impact in November either. That assumes they're back by early November (before the survey week for November payroll data)."
Besides auto assembly and employment data, anything less than a very short strike will affect data on industrial production and capacity utilization, economists said.

"It's clear there will be some pullback in the volume of automobile assemblies because of this CAW strike and there's no doubt this could have a restraining influence for capacity use and production statistics for October," said Sullivan. "As it stands now, the impact would be very, very limited. But if more plants are affected and workers laid off through next week, then the impact would be sizable. Then you're losing a sizable amount of auto assemblies."
Daily spot prices of some sensitive raw materials used in auto production could also be affected, Sullivan said.

"In theory, you could see some decline in demand for these products and that could prompt some softening of sensitive materials prices in the cash markets," he said. "Whether that impacts the PPI (Producer Price Index) depends on how long the strike lasts," he said.
While the production side of the economy will feel the impact of a prolonged auto strike, the demand side of the economy will be less affected, economists said.
Unless the strike is long, the laid-off workers could be back on the job and collecting paychecks again in time for the Christmas buying season.

Talks between GM and the union remained had been deadlocked over the issue of GM's ability to shift work to lower-cost, outside suppliers. But the CAW said Wednesday that GM was ready to recognise limits on the amount of work that can be contracted out.
